prediction.rationale: Six of eight exemplars employ protease-cleavable linkers (dipeptide or tetrapeptide triggers with self-immolative PABC or AM spacers), establishing this as the dominant cleavage strategy for cytotoxic payloads. Plasma stability is a critical differentiator: the EVCit and cBuCit modifications over classical VCit demonstrate that extending or sterically shielding the peptide trigger markedly improves stability (half-life from 2.3 h to 19.1 h; 75% lower free payload), arguing for a 'high' stability priority rather than merely standard. Cysteine bioconjugation via maleimide or maleimidocaproyl handles is the most frequently cited conjugation chemistry, and PEG spacers are employed when the payload is highly hydrophobic (e.g., PBD dimers) to maintain solubility and reduce aggregation.

Different linker chemistry and linker modi ﬁcations have been explored. Maleimide and disul ﬁde linkages represent two major types of linker chemistry. Maleimide has been widely utilized as an antibody connection modality and has been employed with both cleavable or non-cleavable linkers. Accordingly, the pharmacologically efﬁcacious component could be the payload itself or that with partial or full-length linkers depending on the mechanism of action of the payload (Su et al., 2019; Poreba, 2020). Either for cleavable or non- cleavable linkers, the efﬁcient release of the active component would be the desired result, which can be achieved through the optimal linker design. Disulﬁde-based antibody connections have recently been developed as a new strategy f or the generation of cleavable linkers (Pillow et al., 2017; Sadowsky et al., 2017). For both maleimide and disulﬁde cleavable linkers, the steric hindrance created by the proximity of the cleavage site is critical and can be introduced by chemical modiﬁcations to modulate stability of the conjugate. Together, conjugation site, linker length, linkage/conjugation chemistry, cleavable/non-cleavable linkage and steric hindrance are the key parameters for consideration to optimize ADC stability. Under physiological conditions, the interstitial pH of normal tissues and the bloodstream is stable at ≈7.3–7.4.[60] In contrast, the TME is generally more acidic due to increased glucose metabo- lism and poor perfusion, with pH levels dropping to as low as 5.6 in certain tumor types. The drug release trigger determines how the payload is released in response to different conditions, such as enzymes or acidic environments. Since the early 2000s, substantial effort has been directed toward developing technologies to increase linker stability, particularly through alternative types of conjugation chem- istry (Supplementary Figure S1, available at https://doi.org/ 10.1016/j.annonc.2026.04.008). 10 In addition, site-specific conjugation strategies have enabled greater linker stability by using positions less prone to deconjugation and more stable chemistry. 11 These approaches are often, but not invariably, associated with increased homogeneity and higher systemic ADC exposure. ADCs with more stable linkers have repeatedly shown better therapeutic index preclinically, and many programs have advanced into the clinic based on this promise. Yet, clinical evidence to date does not support enhanced linker stability as a standalone driver of improved therapeutic index in patients. In this article, we discuss i) types of linker instability, ii) the evaluation of linker stability using in vitro assays and in vivo pharmacokinetic (PK) analyses and the limitations of pre- clinical models in predicting free payload exposure in humans, iii) our understanding of ADC disposition, and iv) the clinical implications of altering ADC linker stability on clinical maximum tolerated dose (MTD), efficacy, and tolerability. TYPES OF LINKER INSTABILITY The clinical safety and efficacy of an ADC are closely tied to the stability of the linker, which influence when, where, and how the cytotoxic payload is released. 3 It is important to distinguish linker cleavability from linker instability. Linker cleavability depends on specific environmental conditions intended for payload release (i.e. enzymes, reducing condi- tions, pH changes) at tumor site, whereas linker instabilities are defined as spontaneous transformations in circulation. In some cases, both processes can overlap and generate the same species. Notably, noncleavable linkers (i.e. linkers that require full ADC catabolism to release biologically active payload-containing species) are not necessarily stable: for example, MCC-DM1 (e.g. used in trastuzumab emtansine) and MC-MMAF (e.g. used in belantamab mafodotin) show marked instabilities, 12,13 despite being categorized as non- cleavable linkers. Linker instability (Figure 1) 3,14 can be classified into linker- drug instability (instability between the linker and the payload) and antibody-linker instability (instability between the antibody and the linker). 3 Both instabilities result in reduced DAR over time but through the formation of distinct molecular species. ADCs with linker-drug instability release free payload directly into circulation where it may cause toxicity to normal tissue while also contributing to antitumor activity. As such, ISAC technology is designed to selectively deliver immune-stimulating agents to tumor tissues in hopes of engaging our body’s innate and adaptive immune system in the fight against cancer. Due to this indirect mechanism of action, it is not clear that the traditional “rules” of ADC design will apply to the design of ISACs. Indeed, as an illustration of this point, nearly all published ISAC work directly claims that engagement with Fcγ receptors is necessary for activity. 16−18,27,38,39 Moreover, the majority of published ISAC technology employs noncleavable linkers with the implicit assumption that they lack bystander activity and thus will be retained primarily in antigen-presenting myeloid cells after ADCP-mediated uptake. Our study herein is designed to test these assumptions in order to provide critical data for next- generation ISAC programs. We focused our studies on a specific TLR7 agonist known as “E104” that our team reported in 2022. TLR7 agonists are widely known as vaccine adjuvants, specifically activating innate immune pathways present in B-cells, dendritic cells, and myeloid cells. Unlike many toll-like receptors, the expression profile of TLR7 is rather narrow, only being expressed in narrow subsets of immune cells, thus reducing the potential for systemic toxicity (i.e., cytokine release syndrome). Indeed, several systemically delivered TLR7 agonists have entered clinical development 40 �although none have reached approval status. While many tumor-targeting TLR7 agonist designs have been reported in the literature, the work by Ackerman in 2020 promoted a paradigm shift by using ADC technology to deliver TLR7 agonists specifically to tumor tissue. This work ultimately led to two clinical-stage ISACs (BDC-1001 from Bolt Biotherapeutics and NJH-395 from Novartis) that employed a noncleavable linker and a typical FcγR-intact antibody. 16,17 Building on this work, we prepared a set of E104-based tumor-targeting and isotype control ISACs that systematically varied glycosylation status, linker type, and site of conjugation. (Table 1) These conjugates were advanced through a series of functional tests to understand their potency, mechanism of action, and therapeutic potential. The initial focus of our efforts centered on an E104-based ISAC employing a cleavable linker and a deglycosylated (DG) antibody backbone, anti-HER2_(DG/Cys)_mcValCitPABC- E104. We hypothesized that the cleavable linker and highly permeable payload would allow for ablation of FcγR binding affinity without compromising the antitumor efficacy. While this initial design was reported in our 2022 publication, 22 at that time we did not compare this design head-to-head with the industry standard ISAC design (“NJH395-like”) that used a glycosylated Fc domain (FcγR-intact) and a noncleavable linker. Consistent with our prior reports, we found that our redesigned ISAC exhibited potent immunostimulatory activity in coculture assays with mouse and human immune cells and excellent antitumor efficacy in a HER2+ xenograft model. (Figure 2) Both the in vitro and in vivo activity were comparable or better than the industry-standard ISAC Journal of Medicinal Chemistry pubs.acs.org/jmc Article https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jmedchem.5c01908 J. Med. Chem. 2025, 68, 24968−24985 24979 construct. Importantly, we found that the traditional ISAC design induced antigen independent activity, promoting IL-6 and TNFα release in PBMCs (Supporting Figure S2) and modest antitumor activity of the isotype-control ISAC (Figure 2C). In contrast, the redesigned FcγR-ablated/cleavable linker ISAC did not promote cytokine release in PBMC monoculture and the isotype-control ISAC was devoid of antitumor activity. Drugs in the ISAC ISAC is an emerging field and the drugs used are mostly TLR7, TLR8, TLR9 agonists, or STING agonists. Some testing has also been done for other members of the TLR family or any combination (e.g. TLR7/8 dual activation) [37] . Currently, the main ISAC drugs involved include the TLR agonist SBT6050, SBT6290, and BDC-1001; the STING agonist XMT-2056, and the Treg cell regulatory modulators ADCT-301. How - ever, many of these drugs are also defined as ADC by the companies themselves, perhaps it is also because there is not much difference be - tween the appearance of the drug and the technique [38] . The repre - sentative ISAC, BDC-1001, is currently in Phase II clinical trials in patients with HER2-expressing tumors. In addition to the fastest pro - gressing BDC-1001 targeting HER2, ISAC targeting PD-L1 and CEA is also under development. The ISAC targeting PD-L1 achieved essentially complete inhibition when used in C57BL/6 mice at 5mpk (milligrams per kilogram). The antibody to the ISAC partially targets the tumor cells and the TLR agonist carried by the antibody will activate the tumor surrounding DC cells, using the body ’ s innate immune system to kill tumor cells. The Boltbody ™ platform technology reinvigorates the im - mune system of how dendritic cells and other myeloid cells generate effective antitumor immunity [39] . Boltbody ™ ISAC is a unique class of immuno-oncology (IO) therapies, its function is expected to generate systemic immune memory with lasting clinical benefit [15] . Currently, TLR agonists have potential therapeutic promise as one of the research frontier areas in immunotherapy. IRFs (interferon-regulatory factors), whose signaling results in the production of mainly pro-inflammatory cytokines, and type I interferons (IFNs) [41] . ABSTRACT Immune- stimulating antibody conjugates (ISACs) have emerged as a promising class of therapeutics, employing design principles similar to antibody- drug conjugates (ADCs) but replacing cytotoxic payloads with immune- stimulatory agents. These agents enhance immune system activation, enabling more effective tumor targeting and elimination. However, recent clinical setbacks since 2021 have raised concerns about ISACs’ viability as ADC successors. Although ISAC development remains early- stage, clinical trials have revealed significant challenges, including limited efficacy, systemic toxicity (eg, cytokine release syndrome), and anti- drug antibody generation. Current strategies to overcome these hurdles focus on optimizing payload selection (eg, toll- like receptor 7(TLR7) vs stimulator of interferon genes (STING) agonists), improving linker stability, and exploring localized delivery methods. ISACs represent an emerging class of targeted immunotherapeutics designed to overcome limitations of conventional oncology modal- ities. Structurally analogous to ADCs, ISACs comprise a tumor- targeting monoclonal antibody, a chemical linker, and a payload of immune- stimulatory agents (eg, TLR 7/8 or STING agonists) rather than cytotoxic drugs. Its activity appears to be driven by the generation of various pro- inflammatory cytokines, including IFN-α, TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, and IL-8, and also by its ability to recruit and activate dendritic cells. 9 Despite these promising results as a topical agent, systemic administration of Imiquimod has been associated with severe immunological adverse events, thus restricting its application to topical administration for skin-associated cancers. 10 For this reason, there has been a flurry of technologies recently explored for tumor-specific delivery of TLR agonists, including intratumoral injections, nanoparticle formulations, prodrugs cleaved in the tumor microenviron- ment, and (most recently) antibody-conjugates. 11−14 Recent advancements in antibody-drug-conjugate (ADC) technology have enabled the delivery of highly toxic payloads to tumor tissue while minimizing systemic exposure. 15 There are now 12 FDA-approved ADCs that are marketed in the United States, 7 of which are used to treat solid tumors. A related program from Bolt did not report ADA, but rather faced very significant PK problems that severely impeded drug efficacy and resulted in the termination of the clinical trial. 18 Likewise, a TLR8 agonist ISAC program from Silverback resulted in significant immunological toxicities that resulted in termination of the program. 19 The failure of these programs illustrates the need for new approaches for ISAC designs. rule.rationale: Only one exemplar provides concrete linker details: the imidazo-thienopyridine TLR7 agonist ADC uses a Val-Cit dipeptide protease-cleavable linker with stochastic thiol-maleimide conjugation at interchain disulfide cysteines. This is consistent with the need for intracellular (endosomal/lysosomal) release of TLR7/8 agonists, which act on endosomal toll-like receptors, making cathepsin-cleavable dipeptide linkers a logical design choice. However, four of five exemplars lack linker specification, so confidence is low and the rule is extrapolated primarily from a single well-characterized example.

prediction.rationale: Among the exemplars, Val-Cit protease-cleavable linkers consistently enabled efficacious delivery of both siRNA and PMO payloads (DYNE-101, DYNE-251), while the Val-Arg variant failed, suggesting dipeptide identity matters and Val-Cit is preferred. Non-cleavable linkers (SMCC, maleimide) also showed activity (AOC-1001 achieving 80% knockdown, MALAT1 ASO OTV), indicating oligonucleotide payloads can tolerate both cleavable and non-cleavable strategies, but protease-cleavable Val-Cit linkers appear most broadly validated. Shorter disulfide linkers demonstrated improved whole-blood stability over extended analogs, reinforcing that compact linker architecture and high plasma stability are critical design priorities for oligonucleotide ADCs.

In an exon-skipping application, DYNE-251 delivered a PMO using an anti-TfR1 Fab conjugated via a Val-Cit linker. Adminis- tration at 30 mg/kg restored dystrophin expression to over 60% of wild-type levels and reaching 90% in the diaphragm in a DMD mouse model four weeks post-treatment, further underscoring the platform’s capacity to restore functional protein expression [64, 65]. The functional performance of linkers is governed by their physicochemical properties. For cleavable linkers, key stabilization strategies include chemical modi ﬁcations, such as gem-dimethyl substitution in disul ﬁde bonds, and sequence optimization to ﬁne- tune cleavage kinetics. In general, shorter linkers tend to exhibit superior metabolic stability. For instance, AOCs incorporating shorter disulﬁde linkers have demonstrated signi ﬁcantly improved stability in mouse whole blood compared to extended analogs, thereby better preserving the average (drug-to-antibody ratio) [66]. Linker length and conjugation site also substantially in ﬂuence AOC bioactivity, partly by modulating the overall steric conforma- tion of the conjugate [ 67]. These parameters can affect antibody- antigen engagement, oligonucleotide interaction with effector complexes such as RISC, as well as payload release kinetics and oligonucleotide integrity. Experimental evidence indicates that conjugating a non-cleavable linker to the 3 ′or 5 ′end of the siRNA antisense strand has minimal impact on RISC loading, whereas internal modi ﬁcations to the sense strand can markedly compro- mise in vivo activity [ 68]. These observations underscore that in AOC design, linker placement is as critical as linker chemistry, necessitating systematic empirical optimization. Although unmodified siRNA with exposed 2 ′ -OH groups exhibits higher activity in cell culture, engineered partial or complete chemical modifications typically enhance molecular stability while potentially compromising biological activity (F. Wang et al., 2022 ). The most clinically significant modifications include: 2 ′ -O-methyl group substitutions, 2 ′ ,4 ′ -constrained nucleic acid designs, and ribose moiety alterations ( Wittrup and Lieberman, 2015 ). These structural modifications provide two critical benefits. Firstly, they effectively block 2 ′ -OH-mediated hydrolysis, providing strong nuclease resistance. Secondly, they preserve RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) compatibility while significantly reducing immunogenicity ( Anand et al., 2025 ; M. Zhang and Huang, 2022 ). As shown in Fig. 3 ., different types of oligonucleotide modifications can be implemented to achieve superior molecular stability, enhanced resistance to nuclease degradation, and reduced non-specific binding to plasma protein. 3. Mechanism of AOCs AOCs are engineered therapeutics consisting of monoclonal antibody site-specifically linked to sequence-defined oligonucleotide payloads via chemical adapters ( B ¨aumer et al., 2015 ). After the antibody selectively binds to specific receptors on the surface of target cells, the AOC is internalized. Cellular uptake of AOCs is facilitated by multiple endocytic pathways, including clathrin-mediated endocytosis (CME), caveolae-mediated endocytosis, and clathrin-/caveolae-independent mechanisms ( Kalim et al., 2017; Khan and Steeg, 2021; Pei and Buya - nova, 2019 ). Once inside the cell, the oligonucleotide is released to bind to or degrade disease-causing RNA. As shown in Fig. 4 . and Fig. 5 ., antibody-siRNA conjugates and anti-ASO conjugates utilize distinct mechanisms to regulate gene expression( Jiao et al., 2024 ). 3.1. Mechanism of antibody-siRNA conjugates siRNA is a double-stranded RNA molecule approximately 20 25 nucleotides in length. It guides the RISC to target and degrade specific mRNA transcripts ( Raja et al., 2019 ). The mechanism involves: (1) RISC activation: After processing by the cellular enzyme Dicer, the short double-stranded RNA is loaded into the RISC. (2) mRNA degradation: The siRNA guides RISC to bind to the complementary sequence in the target mRNA, leading to its cleavage and degradation. (3) Post-transcriptional regulation: By silencing the target mRNA, siRNA reduces translation and downstream protein synthesis ( Anand et al., 2025; Lehot et al., 2021 ). Cuellar TL et al. utilized THIOMAB ™ antibody conjugates targeting cell-surface antigens to investigate the intracellular trafficking and gene- silencing potential of antibody-RNA conjugates (ARCs). The study demonstrated that antigen-specific internalization can occur through distinct pathways, including slow or non-internalizing routes, recycling endosomes, and lysosomal trafficking. Importantly, they identified components of the endolysosomal system as potentially critical facili - tators of ARC-mediated functional gene silencing ( Cuellar et al., 2015 ). Consistent gene silencing observed with anti-TENB2 ARCs suggests that only a small fraction of internalized siRNA needs to reach the cyto - plasmic RISC complex and undergo strand separation to achieve func - tional silencing. These findings underscore the importance of efficient endosomal trafficking and escape, highlighting the pivotal role of endolysosomal machinery in supporting the intracellular delivery and efficacy of AOC-based therapeutics ( Cuellar et al., 2015 ; G. Tang , 2005 ). 3.2. Mechanism of antibody-ASO conjugates ASOs are short, single-stranded DNA or RNA molecules designed to hybridize with the target mRNA sequence and inhibit gene expression. The mechanisms include: (1) Transcription inhibition: ASOs bind complementarily to the target mRNA to block transcriptional elongation or processing. (2) RNA degradation: ASOs can recruit RNase H1, an endogenous enzyme that degrades the RNA strand of RNA-DNA hybrids, thereby reducing the mRNA levels and their downstream effects. (3) Translation inhibition: By binding to the 5 ′ untranslated region (5 ′ UTR) or coding sequence of the mRNA, ASOs can sterically block ribosome binding or elongation, thereby decreasing protein synthesis (M. Chem. 2025, 68, 6870−6896 Read Online ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations ABSTRACT: Oligonucleotides have emerged as a formidable new class of nucleic acid therapeutics. Fully modified oligonucleotides exhibit enhanced metabolic stability and display successful clinical applicability for targets formerly considered “undruggable”. Accumulating studies show that conjugation to targeting modal- ities of stabilized oligonucleotides, especially small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), has enabled robust delivery to intended cells/ tissues. However, the major challenge in the field has been the stability and targeted delivery of oligonucleotides (siRNAs and antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs)) to extrahepatic tissues. In this Perspective, we review chemistry innovations and emerging delivery approaches that have revolutionized oligonucleotide drug discovery and development. We explore findings from both academia and industry that highlight the potential of oligonucleotides for indications involving different extrahepatic organs� including skeletal muscles, brain, lungs, skin, heart, adipose tissue, and eyes. In all, continued advances in chemistry coupled with conjugation-based approaches or novel administration routes will further advance the delivery of oligonucleotides to extrahepatic tissues. ■ SIGNIFICANCE siRNAs and ASOs have become powerful therapeutic tools, evidenced by a surge in approvals over the past decade. The significance of oligonucleotides for the treatment of rare and common diseases cannot be overstated, considering their precise silencing ability and therapeutic potential. This Perspective presents strategies and examples for applying these modalities to extrahepatic tissues, underscoring the importance of innovative design and delivery in achieving effective oligonucleotide therapeutics. ■ INTRODUCTION The nucleic acid therapeutic (NAT) field has flourished in recent years with the FDA approval of 24 drugs, including small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), ASOs, aptamers, and mRNAs (Figure 1). 1 Of note, 20 of these 24 NATs were approved during the past decade. In particular, the discovery of two classes of oligonucleotides, namely siRNAs and ASOs, has brought to bear the true therapeutic potential of genetic medicines by providing precision therapy (via selective gene silencing) for many diseases. 2 In a landmark Nobel Prize-winning discovery, Fire et al. demonstrated double-stranded siRNA-mediated gene knockdown in Caenorhabditis elegans; they also found that this process was catalytic, thereby requiring only a few molecules of siRNA per cell. 3 Separately, Elbashir et al. showed that a 21-mer siRNA duplex caused sequence-dependent knockdown of mRNA in cultured mammalian cells. 4 The initial example of successful gene silencing in vivo by systemic delivery was demonstrated almost two decades ago. 5 In this seminal study the authors administered cholesterol-conjugated siRNA (for ApoB) iv in mice, and found that cholesterol enabled binding of conjugated siRNA to LDL-C, which subsequently led to ApoB silencing and thereby cholesterol reduction in the liver and jejunum. 5 Further, Davis et al. provided the earliest evidence of gene silencing in humans mediated by systemic administration of nanoparticles encapsulating an siRNA. 6 The primary subcellular location where an siRNA performs its action is the cytoplasm; 2 however, emerging data indicate that it may also operate in the nucleus. 7 The first siRNA therapeutic, Onpattro, was approved by the FDA in 2018; 8 remarkably, it was followed by the approval of five additional siRNA drugs in a span of 5 years. The prevalence of myotonic dystrophy is estimated to be 1 in 20,000 people, 169 and it is caused by a toxic gain-of-function mutation in DMPK mRNA that results in (CUG)n repeats. Patients with DM1 have CUG repeats ranging from the hundreds to the thousands, and this corelates with the severity of the disease (Figure 4). These repeats form hairpin structures that bind and sequester muscle blind-like protein (MBNL), which is essential for splicing (Figure 4). Sequestration of MBNL causes aberrant splicing of multiple mRNAs in myotubes, thus driving the muscular disease condition in patients with DM1. In NHPs, Avidity’s team estimated that their siRNA for DMPK has an EC 50 of 100 pM, suggestive of a robust potency of siRNA at low doses. Drugs in phase 1/2 clinical studies from Avidity displayed favorable safety and tolerability profiles in patients with DM1. 170 Furthermore, administration of AOC 1001 in patients resulted in a dose-dependent increase of siRNA in muscles, which ultimately led to a mean reduction of 42% of DMPK mRNA (after 6 weeks) following a single dose of 1 mg/kg or two doses of 2 mg/kg or 4 mg/kg. 170 It has been speculated that AOC 1001 operates in the nucleus, which may be supported by recent results from the Corey laboratory that showed the presence of Argonaut 2 and RISC factors in the cell nuclei. 7 In addition, Avidity’s data revealed that DMPK knockdown is associated with normalization of splicing 171 and subsequent enhancement of clinical activity. 170 Remarkably, multiple dosing of 4 mg/kg of AOC 1001 led to improvements in myotonia and total muscle strength that translated into coordinated functioning of muscles in patients with DM1. 170 Because of these promising clinical data, AOC 1001 has advanced to phase 3 clinical trials. This evaluation has allowed us to optimize siRNA chemistries, select linkers, identify points of conjugation on the antibody and siRNA, develop strategies to conjugate an antibody to an siRNA oligonucleotide, and understand the impact of oligonucleotide-to-antibody ratios on AOC activity. Our findings show the importance of selecting appropriate siRNA chemical modifications to improve tissue delivery in vivo and achieve higher target gene KD in tissues of interest. Our platform can accommodate various points of conjugation on the antibody, offering flexibility to choose between cysteine, site-specific cysteine, and sugar conjugations. Initial studies indicate that lysine conjugates are not optimal for AOCs, but additional studies are needed to understand the differences. The siRNA-to-antibody ratio is limited to 1, likely due to high charge of each siRNA and the potential phosphorothioate- mediated nonspecific binding of DAR ≥ 2 AOCs. The AOC platform can accommodate most noncleavable linker chem- istries when conjugated on both ends of the sense strand, indicating that remnants of linker attached to the released siRNA sense strand, after AOC digestion in lysosomes, may not interfere with Ago2 protein binding and RISC loading. We found no significant differences in plasma PK, siRNA tissue delivery, and target gene KD between noncleavable linkers like MCC, BisMal, CB, and MB with rapidly internalized αmTfR1 AOCs. Additional evaluation with AOCs that show longer plasma PK are needed to tease out any differences between these noncleavable linkers. Results from our evaluation of cleavable linkers demonstrate that AOCs with less sterically hindered disulfide linkers like PDP, MPT and SS(methyl) are less stable than more sterically hindered disulfide SS(gem- dimethyl). The reduced plasma clearance of AOCs correlated with the increasing steric hindrance around the disulfide bond. The VC linker offered no significant improvement over stable MCC or BisMal linkers, indicating the tolerance for remnant linker attached to siRNA for Ago2 binding and RISC loading. The exploration of conjugation positions, other than 5′ or 3′ end positions on the sense strand, on both strands of siRNA also revealed that the internal conjugation locations show lower activity than the 5′ end conjugation. This is likely due to interference of siRNA duplex interaction with either Ago2 protein or RISC loading. Addition of 5000 molecular weight PEG on the other side of siRNA in an AOC, by sandwiching siRNA between antibody and PEG, showed approximately three-fold improved tissue delivery to the targeted tumor cells with αhPSMA AOC and a five-fold increase in muscle with αmTfR1 AOC. The increased delivery of siRNA resulted in higher target gene KD. PEG is likely providing steric shielding to nucleases and may reduce nonspecific protein binding of AOC. Overall, our SAR study provides important insights into the design and optimization of siRNA AOCs, identifying key factors that can influence PK, tissue delivery, and efficacy of these complex bioconjugates. These findings are consistent across multiple antibody targets and siRNAs, suggesting these design principles can be applied to the entire AOC class. By understanding the SAR of AOCs, researchers can continue to develop new and improved therapeutics for a range of diseases and conditions. ■ EXPERIMENTAL SECTION siRNA Synthesis. These conjugates can be optimized for improved delivery and mRNA knockdown (KD) through understanding of structure−activity relationships. In this study, we systematically examined factors including antibody isotype, siRNA chemistry, linkers, conjugation chemistry, PEGy- lation, and drug-to-antibody ratios (DARs) for their impact on bioconjugation, pharmacokinetics (PK), siRNA delivery, and bioactivity. Conjugation site (cysteine, lysine, and Asn297 glycan) and DAR proved critical for optimal conjugate PK and siRNA delivery. SiRNA chemistry including 2′ sugar modifications and positioning of phosphorothioates were found to be critical for delivery and duration of action. By utilizing cleavable and noncleavable linkers, we demonstrated the impact of linkers on PK and mRNA KD. To achieve optimal properties of antibody−siRNA conjugates, a careful selection of siRNA chemistry, DAR, conjugation sites, linkers, and antibody isotype is necessary. ■ INTRODUCTION Antibodies and oligonucleotides, two powerful classes of molecules, have diverse applications in biology and medicine. As highly specific proteins, antibodies recognize and bind to a wide range of targets. Their proven effectiveness as receptor antagonists and as delivery vehicles for small molecules makes them potent therapeutics. 1−4 Oligonucleotides exert their therapeutic effect through multiple mechanisms, including inducing the degradation of mRNA or promoting splice modulation. 5−9 Over the last 25 years, more than 16 oligonucleotide therapeutics have been approved for multiple therapeutic indications, including homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, spinal muscular atrophy, Duchenne muscular dystrophy, hereditary trans- thyretin-mediated amyloidosis, familial chylomicronemia syn- drome, acute hepatic porphyria, and primary hyperoxaluria. 10 Small interfering ribonucleic acids (siRNAs) are 20−25 nucleotide-long, double-stranded RNA molecules containing a complementary sense and antisense strand. When inside the cell, these duplexes load into the Ago2 protein. Following this, the sense strand of the duplex siRNA is cleaved, and its fragments ejected, leaving behind a functional RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) that comprises the antisense strand and Ago2. The RISC then uses the antisense strand to recognize and bind to complementary mRNA sequences within the cell. Once fully hybridized with the mRNA, Ago2 cleaves the mRNA between target bases 10 and 11, resulting in mRNA degradation and reduced gene expression. siRNAs are proven therapeutic agents, especially in diseases caused by the overexpression of certain genes or the presence of harmful genetic mutations. By selectively targeting specific disease- related RNA, siRNA-based therapies hold promise for treating a wide range of conditions, including certain types of cancer, viral infections, and genetic disorders. 5−9 siRNA therapeutics face three main challenges: selectivity, stability, and delivery. MOLECULAR CHARACTERISTICS OF AOCS AOC combines oligonucleotides with gene regulatory functions to targeted antibodies through covalent linkage, aiming to achieve efﬁcient intracellular delivery of oligonucleotides to speci ﬁc cells for precise regulation of target gene expression. Structurally, AOC resembles antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), both comprising three components: an antibody, a linker, and an active payload. However, due to fundamental differences in delivery objectives and payload properties, AOC exhibits distinct design principles compared to ADCs. We systematically compare the design differences between the two conjugates as shown in Table 2. The core function of AOC lies in utilizing antibodies to deliver gene-regulating oligonucleotides into cells, enabling precise regulation of gene expression at the mRNA level. This fundamen- tally differs from traditional cytotoxic ADCs, which deliver cell toxins to directly kill target cells. The target receptors of AOC prioritize endocytic ef ﬁciency and high circulation properties over mere speci ﬁcity. The antibody-linker combination must balance speciﬁc binding af ﬁnity with endosomal escape capability — a critical factor determining gene silencing ef ﬁcacy. Chemical modiﬁcations to the oligonucleotide enhance stability and modulate immunogenicity while preserving long-acting therapeu- tic properties. Therefore, the creation of AOC drugs is a precision- engineered system that integrates gene regulation, endosomal escape, and targeted endocytosis. TARGETED RECEPTORS AND THERAPEUTIC INDICATIONS The therapeutic ﬁeld selection for AOCs is fundamentally determined by the tissue distribution speci ﬁcity and endocytosis kinetics of their target receptors. A mature target receptor is crucial for the successful development of AOCs, serving not only as a “navigation system ” for precise oligonucleotide delivery to target cells but also directly de ﬁning the drug ’s potential indications. The therapeutic potential of antibody-nucleic acid conjugates in a variety of disease areas, from hematologic malignancies and solid tumor immunotherapy to hereditary muscle disorders and liver diseases, has been preliminarily demonstrated by current research and application of receptors like TfR1, ASGPR, CD22, and SIRP α. Interestingly, AOCs ’ payload activity goes beyond conventional gene silencing to include immune activation, splicing regulation, and other modalities. Nevertheless, the target tissues that the antibody moiety de ﬁnes continue to determine their effective function. Therefore, the logical design of AOCs depends on an awareness of the inherent link between “receptor-tissue-disease”. This chapter will explore this fundamental link, highlight important receptor targets that are currently being studied, and show how a mature, validated receptor can act as a tailored delivery platform for AOCs, propelling drug development in a variety of therapeutic domains. rule.rationale: Among the exemplars, Val-Cit protease-cleavable linkers consistently enabled efficacious delivery of both siRNA and PMO payloads (DYNE-101, DYNE-251), while the Val-Arg variant failed, suggesting dipeptide identity matters and Val-Cit is preferred. Non-cleavable linkers (SMCC, maleimide) also showed activity (AOC-1001 achieving 80% knockdown, MALAT1 ASO OTV), indicating oligonucleotide payloads can tolerate both cleavable and non-cleavable strategies, but protease-cleavable Val-Cit linkers appear most broadly validated. Shorter disulfide linkers demonstrated improved whole-blood stability over extended analogs, reinforcing that compact linker architecture and high plasma stability are critical design priorities for oligonucleotide ADCs.
